I would give every person a reliably active sense of empathy—the ability to feel, not just understand, how our choices affect others, including future generations and the natural world.

Why this one change?

1. Root-cause leverage  
   • Poverty, war, climate inaction, discrimination and corruption all persist, in part, because decision-makers can insulate themselves from the consequences of their actions. If that insulation vanished, the incentives that drive harmful behavior would shift.

2. Self-reinforcing  
   • Empathy begets cooperation. Once people experience positive feedback from fairer, more collaborative systems, they tend to protect and spread them, making the change durable.

3. Non-zero-sum  
   • Unlike resources, empathy doesn’t run out when shared. Widening the circle of concern costs nothing yet raises overall well-being.

4. Multigenerational reach  
   • A stronger felt connection to future people would make long-term risks—climate change, biodiversity loss, unaligned AI—politically urgent today.

What might a more empathetic world look like?

• Policy: Budgets would be drafted with “future impact statements,” and social safety nets would be viewed not as charity but as mutual insurance.  
• Business: Success metrics would weigh social and environmental externalities alongside profit.  
• Technology: Products would be designed for inclusivity and sustainability by default.  
• Culture: Media, education and even urban design would emphasize perspective-taking—dialogue across divides, immersive history, service learning.

Is empathy teachable?

Yes, though imperfectly. Techniques include early-childhood emotional literacy, facilitated cross-group contact, narrative storytelling, mindfulness practices that reduce self-focus, and institutional norms that reward prosocial behavior. The science isn’t magic, but it’s real: regular use of these tools measurably increases generosity, reduces prejudice, and supports cooperative problem-solving.

Why not pick a concrete fix like “cure malaria” or “invent fusion power”?

Those would be magnificent, but they’re narrower. A world that feels responsible for one another would unlock broader, compounding solutions—including the money, political will and creativity needed to cure diseases and deploy clean energy.

In short, if I could pull only one lever, I’d choose the one most likely to move every other lever: universal, lived empathy.
